glossary.Systemic: Affecting the whole body rather than one local area.
glossary.Hypersensitivity: An exaggerated or inappropriate immune response that damages the body's own tissues.
glossary.Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, causing redness, warmth and a fall in blood pressure.
glossary.Vasoconstriction: Narrowing of blood vessels, raising blood pressure and reducing swelling.
glossary.Bronchoconstriction: Narrowing of the airways due to tightening of the bronchial smooth muscle.
glossary.Vascular permeability: How leaky vessel walls are; when raised, fluid escapes into tissues and causes swelling.
glossary.Penicillin: A beta-lactam antibiotic and one of the commonest drug causes of anaphylaxis.
glossary.Amoxicillin: A penicillin antibiotic; can trigger anaphylaxis in penicillin-allergic patients.
glossary.Latex: Natural rubber in gloves and catheters, a recognised anaphylaxis trigger.
glossary.Hoarse voice: A rough, croaky voice, here a sign of swelling around the larynx.
glossary.Poor perfusion: Too little blood reaching the tissues, seen as cold, pale, mottled skin and confusion.
glossary.Hypoxia: Too little oxygen reaching the tissues.
glossary.Hypotension: Low blood pressure, here from widespread vasodilation and fluid leak.
glossary.Respiratory distress: Visible hard work of breathing: fast rate, recession, nasal flaring, use of accessory muscles.
glossary.Inspiratory: Happening when breathing in; inspiratory stridor points to upper airway narrowing.
glossary.Expiratory: Happening when breathing out; expiratory wheeze points to lower airway narrowing.
glossary.Paradoxical: Moving the opposite way to normal, as when chest and abdomen move out of sync.
glossary.Airway obstruction: Blockage of the airway, here from swelling of the tongue, lips or larynx.
glossary.mcg: Microgram: one thousandth of a milligram.
glossary.SC: Subcutaneous: an injection into the fat just under the skin.
glossary.IM: Intramuscular: an injection given into a muscle.
glossary.Three-point patient ID: Checking name, date of birth and hospital number before giving any treatment.
glossary.Nebulised: Turned into a fine mist that is breathed in through a mask.
glossary.Bronchodilators: Drugs such as salbutamol that relax airway muscle and open the airways.
glossary.Antihistamines: Drugs that block histamine receptors, easing itch and urticaria; not life-saving in anaphylaxis.
glossary.Resus: The resuscitation area or team for critically unwell patients.
glossary.IV fluid bolus: A rapid infusion of fluid into a vein to restore blood pressure.
glossary.IV adrenaline infusion: Continuous adrenaline into a vein, used only by experts for refractory anaphylaxis.
glossary.Hypoxic: Having low oxygen levels in the blood or tissues.
glossary.Shocked: In circulatory shock: blood pressure too low to perfuse the organs.
glossary.Risk-stratified: Sorting patients by their risk to decide who needs admission and who can go home.
glossary.Allergy clinic: A specialist service that confirms the trigger and plans long-term avoidance and treatment.
glossary.Contractility: How forcefully the heart muscle squeezes with each beat.
glossary.Bronchodilation: Widening of the airways when bronchial smooth muscle relaxes.
glossary.Oedema: Swelling caused by fluid leaking into the tissues.
glossary.Mucosal oedema: Swelling of the moist lining of the airway, narrowing it.
glossary.Inflammatory cells: White blood cells, such as eosinophils and neutrophils, drawn in to a site of inflammation.
glossary.Retrospective: Looking back afterwards; tryptase confirms anaphylaxis after the event.
glossary.Clinical diagnosis: A diagnosis made from history and examination, without needing a test to confirm it.
glossary.Cross-links: When an allergen binds two neighbouring IgE molecules at once, triggering mast cell release.
glossary.Shellfish: Prawns, crab, lobster and similar foods, a common food trigger of anaphylaxis.
glossary.Hypoxaemia: Low oxygen level in the arterial blood.
